questions.question_text:
Equal rectangles show $\frac{3}{7}$ and $\frac{5}{7}$ shaded.
Which has more shaded area?

options.why: This treats the smaller shaded count as the larger fraction.
The wholes match but the shaded part counts differ.

questions.question_text:
Two equal-sized bars are divided into equal parts. Bar A has $3$ of $6$ parts shaded and bar B has $2$ of $4$ parts shaded.
Compare the shaded fractions.

options.text: Bar A has the greater shaded fraction.
options.why: This compares only the shaded counts, treating $3>2$ as enough to decide despite the different part sizes.

options.text: Bar B has the greater shaded fraction.
options.why: This compares only the size of each part, ignoring that A has more of its smaller parts shaded.

questions.question_text: Which model represents the greater fraction: $6$ of $9$ counters or $5$ of $9$ counters?

options.why: This selects the smaller numerator for equal-sized collections.
The denominators match but the marked counts do not.

questions.question_text:
A strip shows $\frac{2}{3}$ shaded.
Which fraction would shade the same area on an equal strip split into twelfths?

options.why: This keeps the numerator while changing the part size.
This models one half rather than two thirds.

questions.question_text:
Two equal-sized area models are divided into equal parts. Model A has $7$ of $12$ parts shaded and model B has $3$ of $4$ parts shaded.
A student says A has the greater shaded fraction because $7>3$.
What is correct?

options.why: This compares shaded counts without accounting for different totals.
This changes fourths to twelfths by adding $8$ to the denominator and incorrectly adding $4$ to the numerator, turning $\frac{3}{4}$ into $\frac{7}{12}$.

questions.question_text:
Models show $\frac{6}{8}$ and $\frac{9}{12}$ of equal wholes.
What comparison is true?

options.why: This compares numerators while ignoring different part sizes.
This compares denominators without simplifying the fractions.
